title: How is a partition stored on disk (segment files, offset index), and how does retention/compaction interact with segments?
shortTitle: How is a partition stored on disk (segment files, offset index), and how does retention/compaction interact with segments?
keyPoints: A partition is a directory of segment triples: .log (data), .index (offset index), .timeindex (time index).
Only the active (newest) segment is written to; closed segments are immutable.
The offset index is a sparse map from logical offset to byte position for fast lookups via binary search.
Segments roll when they hit segment.bytes or segment.ms, whichever comes first.
Delete retention removes whole closed segments; compaction rewrites closed segments to latest-per-key.
The active segment is never eligible for retention or compaction.
Segment size is a trade-off: smaller gives finer cleanup but more file-handle and index overhead.

s1_definition.oneliner: A partition is a directory of immutable closed segments plus one active segment, each paired with an offset index and a time index; retention deletes whole aged segments while compaction rewrites them to latest-per-key.
s1_definition.profdef:
A Kafka partition is stored on disk as a directory of log segment files with matching indexes.

- **Segment file (.log)** – holds a contiguous range of records by offset, typically up to 1 GB.
- **Offset index (.index)** – a sparse map from logical offset to byte position in the .log file, enabling fast binary-search lookups.
- **Time index (.timeindex)** – a sparse map from timestamp to offset, powering time-based seeks and retention.
- **Active segment** – the newest segment that is still being written to; closed segments are immutable.
- **Segment rolling** – the active segment is closed and a new one opened when it hits `segment.bytes` or `segment.ms`.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps a partition's transaction history in a filing cabinet. Each drawer is a segment holding consecutive entries. Each drawer has a small index card on the front that says entry number so-and-so starts at this spot (the offset index), and a second card mapping dates to entry numbers (the time index). Clerks only add new entries to the front drawer that is currently open. Older drawers are sealed. When cleaning up, the bank either throws out whole sealed drawers that are too old (retention) or rewrites them to keep only the latest entry per account (compaction), never touching the open drawer.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Partition Directory: /data/kafka/settlements-0/

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Segment 0 (closed, immutable)                        │
  │  00000000000000000000.log       (records 0-1048575)   │
  │  00000000000000000000.index     (offset -> byte pos)  │
  │  00000000000000000000.timeindex (timestamp -> offset)  │
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Segment 1 (closed, immutable)                        │
  │  00000000000001048576.log       (records 1048576-...) │
  │  00000000000001048576.index                           │
  │  00000000000001048576.timeindex                        │
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Active Segment (open, being written to)               │
  │  00000000000002097152.log       ← producers append    │
  │  00000000000002097152.index                           │
  │  00000000000002097152.timeindex                        │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Offset Index (sparse):
  ┌────────┬────────────┐
  │ Offset │ Byte Pos   │
  ├────────┼────────────┤
  │    0   │       0    │
  │  100   │   32768    │  ← binary search finds nearest
  │  200   │   65536    │     entry, then scan forward
  │  300   │   98304    │
  └────────┴────────────┘

  Cleanup:
  Delete retention: whole closed segment removed
  Compaction:       closed segment rewritten (latest per key)
  Active segment:   NEVER touched by cleanup
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A Kafka partition is stored on disk as a directory of log segment files. Each segment is a .log file holding records in offset order, paired with a sparse .index offset index and a .timeindex time index, all named by the segment's base offset. Only the active segment is written to; closed segments are immutable, and that immutability is the foundation that makes cleanup safe.

The offset index enables fast lookups without scanning gigabyte files. It maps logical offsets to byte positions at regular intervals, so Kafka binary-searches the index, seeks to the right spot, and scans forward a short distance. The time index does the same for timestamps, powering time-based seeks and retention decisions.

Retention and compaction both operate at segment granularity on closed segments and always skip the active segment. Delete retention removes whole segments when their records age out. Compaction rewrites closed segments to keep only the latest record per key, preserving offsets and leaving gaps. On the National Bank of India settlement topic, Pankaj's team uses delete retention so old history is trimmed by dropping whole aged segments, while the account-state topic uses compaction so the latest balance per account is always retained.

Remember one sentence: a partition is a sequence of immutable segments plus one active segment, each with a sparse offset and time index, and all cleanup is segment-oriented.
